We have the field offices -- my mission is covering the whole territory of former Yugoslavia, so we have field offices in Zagreb, in Belgrade now -- that was a good achievement -- and in Skopje and then we have in Mostar, Sarajevo, Banja Luka -- that is new too -- and so those are spread, so we have in Zagreb and Belgrade and Skopje too of the field officers. So we do not have very much of staff to work with, but our work is going on from the fact that we should co-operate. We have all the time been listening to this lack of co-operation in the international community and the humanitarian work and human rights work, but we have a very good co-operation with other organisations. The International Red Cross is one of our main friends in the activities, ECMM, OSCE, of course UNHCR. All of us are giving details to each other and then we are checking by interviews, is that information right or wrong. So this is the way that we have been doing this. So this estimates about killed and possibly killed, that could not escape. They are very much in co-operation with the International Red Cross where we could come up even to 8,000 killed but, for sure, at least 3,000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You spoke of children. According to the testimonies we had in Srebrenica and otherwise, only men between 16 and 60 were taken in buses to the execution places or otherwise, but no mention was made of children. Did you come across also the torture of children and the execution of children?

utterances.speaker: MS. REHN
utterances.text: I heard about children under the age of 16, at least boys of 15, that had been taken because their mothers have been telling about this, and I have no reason to doubt their information. So, certainly, there were younger too. But, directly, to take small children to these buses or away from the buses, I do not think that happened. Instead, we have, of course, the reports of mother who kept her child and then that child, a little one, was directly killed with a knife and things like that that are, of course, terrible to be listening to. But I cannot state that I should add information that many younger than 16 should have been taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So no evidence that there has been extermination of children?

utterances.speaker: MS. REHN
utterances.text: No, no, we cannot absolutely not in a real scale; there can have been single cases and that is bad enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned rape as one of the forms of ethnic cleansing. Did you reach a conclusion that it was used effectively as a means of ethnic cleansing and how?

utterances.speaker: MS. REHN
utterances.text: In that sense, this is a combination of all the terror to make people leave their homes, to just escape from their homes during all this conflict. There were so many of these methods, as I said, forced labour, looting, burning, and all this, but rape was one matter that was very much used. It was used, as I said, by many parties in this. I met in Banja Luka with an organisation of raped women. I am very sorry that there must be organisations for raped women; that is not telling very well about the world we are living in. They wanted to meet me. There were a couple of young girls with them too. They came from different parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There were different so-called nationalities too, ethnics there. They wanted to speak to me, woman to woman. I must say that what I heard was really the worst I have been listening to. The way the soldiers had raped women in front of their children and that was, perhaps, the worst for them. That was something that should not really happen. That was one part of this, to make people to leave their homes because they could not stay any more. They were frightened. They were afraid, especially those who were living alone, women alone; how much they even locked their doors, they could not been sure not in the night there should be intruders coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. REHN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, just a few brief questions: with regard to Mr. Mazowiecki's report, you stated an opinion at the outset, you said he was quite unpleased and that you shared that feeling. Now you have just arrived. Could you tell us that why right from the outset you could go along with his view of the matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. REHN
utterances.text: Sorry, now I missed something. I was late with the interpretation. If your Honour could say -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: When you began this afternoon, you indicated how you replaced Mr. Mazowiecki at the head of the Commission. You said that he was quite upset when he left and you said that you shared those feelings. You had just arrived in that position. So, how was that that you came to share that feeling right from the outset?

utterances.speaker: MS. REHN
utterances.text: Because, first of all, I honoured him as a person very much. When I had read his reports, because, of course, before I started I tried to have some kind of knowledge of what I am going in to -- perhaps I did not know enough though, but now I know what I am up to -- and I especially shared the view that you should make something dramatic, so that the eyes of the rest of the world should be focused on things that are happening like this Srebrenica case, because I learnt so much about this from the very beginning. So I absolutely was capable of sharing his views, even not being there when it happened. Only those who had to escape from there, of course, are the real ones to know that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Still in relation to the Commission: since you have been there, you have been reviewing matters, looking at the missions, now since September 1995 have you had to correct the conclusions by Mr. Mazowiecki, and do you think there are any mistakes or some things that are not quite right that you might want to bring up before the court, or do you think, on the contrary, that there are not things that need any correcting?

utterances.speaker: MS. REHN
utterances.text: This was a very tricky question, your Honour, but I do not have the need to correct Tadeusz Mazowiecki and I even believe that I should not do that. But, of course, things are proceeding and something that could be evident then, perhaps, there will be new evidence coming later on. I have not found so far any new evidence of that kind, but I cannot exclude that from the possibilities, that there will be new evidence that something, perhaps, was not correct, totally correct. But what he has been telling in his report has been very detailed. Like in my own two reports, there have been very detailed paragraphs exactly telling how things were happening, how they proceeded, how many were taken, how many were drowned when they were forced to be expelled over a river -- that was in October -- and they just drowned old people who could not swim. All these things have been explained by me very detailed. The same was the method of his. So these details are, of course, not to be corrected but, as your Honour said, that the conclusions perhaps could be wrong. They were the right conclusions then. I have to make my conclusions now in a new situation. We must remember that he worked before the Dayton Agreement. Now there is the willingness from all parties to try to do something, though positive, I hope at least there is the willingness that all parties want to do something positive out of this. So, the circumstances have really changed for my part. So, if there will be new findings, I will give them in my reports, but not in the sense that I am correcting the very honourable Tadeusz Mazowiecki.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You were appointed in September 1995, so three months after the events in Srebrenica. Srebrenica, could that have been avoided?

utterances.speaker: MS. REHN
utterances.text: We all hope so, but I have been reading the reports, as I said, about Srebrenica, also the Dutch governmental report of 100-something pages. I have to admit, because I was so much involved with peacekeeping during my years as Defence Minister, so I know very well the rules of peacekeeping, and I find this as a very, very bad mixture of civilian and military operation where, like for the air strikes and the air protection, it was a mass of orders that should be gone through with Mr. Akashi giving the final permission to this and with just ping-ponging these decisions among military and civilians. So it prolonged the procedure so much to be really efficient. I have tried to look at the Dutch Battalion and their behaviour, how much they could have been doing more. I cannot blame the single soldier, the single peace keeper. I wonder if they took their mandate though in some way too exactly, not to use power only for self-defence, as this is the rule for peacekeeping operations, because perhaps if there should have been more of this forceful, just behaviour, perhaps then there could have been another outcome. But that is the theories and speculations. The only thing I know, that it was badly prepared from UN altogether, from the leadership of UN in that sense, that you should not create safe areas if you cannot protect them. The Secretary General asked for much more troops from the very beginning so that they could be protected, but the nations, all of us who are providing troops, we did not give more of these troops. So everybody knew that there was not protection enough for these safe areas. So all these together, of course, could give the answer that we could have -- there could have been no Srebrenica if things should have gone right, but I believe too that now our responsibility is to find the answers to those who escaped Srebrenica. We owe them, owe that to those who did not escape.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have one last question before you leave. You talked about the involvement of the church, the moral authorities who, in your view, did not have any effective moderation. Now you go to the field, you are telling us about the future. Do you have the feeling that amid the people in these territories that there is a change in people's attitudes, that there has been a change of heart, that this sorrowful war has made people change their mentalities, their minds, or do you have the feeling that it is just a matter of time before the weapons will be firing again? What is your feeling? That is my last question.

utterances.speaker: MS. REHN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I have, though, the feeling that just the common people, the ordinary people, they want peace. They absolutely want peace. I rely specially (and I am absolutely no feminist), but I rely very much on the women because there are NGOs that are absolutely fantastic, women organisations of different kind, youth organisations and so on who are now telling that, "Now we are taking the things in our hands. We are not relying upon the leadership any more, the leadership who started the war, who went on with the war and is the one who is now negotiating around the tables, the same persons". So they want really to take very much over. If we can support them and there, and I know this is not the same question for this courtroom, but if we can support those organisations that are starting from the very grass roots, giving just some kind of expressions of the feelings of the people, the civilians there, the citizens, then perhaps there is a good future. But if all those who do not like the peace to come, if they will have the power, then it is, of course, the opposite direction. But if I may conclude with optimism, I believe more in these peaceful powers than in those that are break down peace.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So at one point you sounded pessimistic, but you finished up on an optimistic note which is welcome. So thank you very much for accepting our invitation. Now I would like to turn to counsel for the Prosecution to see whether the Prosecution has any questions for Mrs. Rehn?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. From the side of the Prosecution, we have been listening with the greatest interest to Mrs. Rehn's presentation. We also thank her for coming, but we have no questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mrs. Rehn, the Tribunal would like to thank you again. The usher will accompany you out. Thank you again. (Mrs. Rehn withdrew)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Counsel for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ostberg, would you like to show in the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: We are ready. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, our next witness, we call Drazen Erdemovic. DRAZEN ERDEMOVIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, would you like to remind us of what Drazen Erdemovic's present situation is in respect of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Erdemovic has entered a guilty plea in proceedings relating to the indictment that was confirmed against him. He has been scheduled for a sentencing hearing and the sentencing hearing has been continued to a further date yet to be decided.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If Mr. Drazen Erdemovic could be given a head set and please do that whenever we have a witness. Do you hear me, Mr. Erdemovic? Can you hear me? Fine. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can you hear me in your language? You can hear me in Serbo-Croatian, sir? Can you hear me, Mr. Erdemovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I cannot hear the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let us see if we can straighten out these technical details. Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You hear me in Serbo-Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Please read the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Drazen Erdemovic, you accepted the summons to appear as a witness in the case against Messrs. Karadzic and Mladic and that was at the request of the Prosecution. You reiterated your willingness to testify at a recent review of your status. I would like things to be quite clear. The sentencing procedure has been deferred because we have asked for some further medical information. But now you are here as a witness for the Prosecution. You have indicated that you are willing to testify. Your counsel, with your agreement and with your interests at heart, also wished you to testify. There are some very specific Rules within our Rules of Procedure and Evidence that state that an accused may, of course, testify and that might be taken into consideration in future deliberations. The presentencing procedure, as I said, the sentencing procedure was deferred. Now we are going to hear what Mr. Harmon has to say. Please proceed, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Thank you very much. (To the witness): Mr. Erdemovic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you please state your name and spell your last name for the record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my name is Drazen Erdemovic, E-R-D-E-M-O-V-I-C. I was born on 25th November 1971 in Tuzla and I am Croat by origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, before joining the Bosnian Serb Army were you a member of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How long did you serve in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a year, that was my regular service, and four months on the reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, if you could move just a little closer to the microphone, that would be helpful. Thank you. What were your duties and responsibilities in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was with the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When did you leave the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you eventually join the Bosnian Serb Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you eventually join the army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, when I left my military service the war had begun in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I was called up sometime in July 1992 to join the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: OK. I was getting ahead of that part of your testimony, but please you can explain that part as well. Please explain the sequence of events that led you to join ultimately the Bosnian Serb Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have just said, in July, I was called up and I went to join the army, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina I spent some three months. After that, in Tuzla, the Croat Defence Council was formed and I also received summons and I went to the Croat Defence Council and I was assigned to police, to a police station, in the place called Breske near Tuzla. In the Croat Defence Council, in there, I was on sometime I believe until 3rd November 1993. On 3rd November 1993, I moved from Tuzla to the Republika Srpska. Since I have moved from Tuzla with my wife and found myself in the Republika Srpska, I needed a man whom I had already helped and who is of Serb ethnicity, I needed his help to get to Switzerland because he had sons there who had worked there for a long time. However, the man did not keep his word and because I needed a status of some kind, since I was a Croat in the Republika Srpska, so as to be eligible to qualify for some accommodation, I had to join the army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When did you join that army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I joined that army some four times later after my arrival in the Republika Srpska or, to be more precise, sometime in April 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: To what unit were you assigned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I reported to the military command in Bijeljina and I was offered two possibilities or, rather, two units. I went to a unit which already included some Croats and Muslim, Muslims and Slovene.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ultimately, what unit did you join?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That unit had no name at the time. It was attached to the Chiefs of Staff and General headquarters of the army of Republika Srpska and later on it was named the 10th Sabotage Unit of the army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What type of unit was that and what types of activities was it engaged in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a reconnaissance unit responsible for the reconnaissance in the territories held by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we went into the depths of their territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What were your duties and responsibilities in that unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the outset, I engaged in reconnaissance in the territory familiar to me, that is, in the direction of the town of Tuzla. Later on after that, I became the Sergeant. I was the Commander of the 1st Sabotage group in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ultimately, when you left that unit, was the highest rank that you achieved the rank of Sergeant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I only wish to say that I spent two -- that for two months I was the Commander of the group and I had the rank of a Sergeant, but I ended up being demoted because I disagreed with some decisions of my superiors. They demoted me and I was also no longer the Commander of the 1st Sabotage group. After some disagreements, after a mission which I had said I did not want that mission accomplished because it concerned, because it would involve human casualties, human victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the time of the Bosnian Serb attack on Srebrenica, who was the commanding officer of the 10th Sabotage unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Its Commander was Milorad Pelemis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: To whom in the Bosnian Serb Army chain of command did Lieutenant Pelemis report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He accounted to Colonel Salapura of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where was Colonel Salapura assigned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought I said he was reconnaissance officer in the headquarters of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say the "headquarters", are you saying that he was assigned to the intelligence centre of the main staff at Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So, as I understand it, Mr. Erdemovic, your particular sabotage unit was directly subordinate to the main staff of the Bosnian Serb Army in Han Pijesak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was your reconnaissance unit the only one of its kind that was attached to the main staff of the Bosnian Serb Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now at the time of the attack in Srebrenica in July 1995, how many men were assigned to your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our detachment had 60 people or thereabouts, I would not know exactly, but during the attack of Srebrenica there were, I think, 35 men participated in that others were on another mission, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, on 10th July, did your unit receive orders to participate in the Bosnian Serb operation against the enclave of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What were your orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 10th July we arrived in the barracks and we had briefings between 1815 and we were told then to get ready because a few hours later we were to set off towards Zvornik. When we arrived in Zvornik, we were told to go on to Bratunac and await further orders there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you receive additional orders, Mr. Erdemovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We received further orders. We left Bratunac in the direction of Srebrenica and there we stayed on a hill, on an elevation, and there we spent the night, on 10th July. Then our Commander, Milorad Pelemis, told us we will spend the night there and he would come in the morning with new orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When he arrived with new orders, was that on the morning of 11th July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What were your new orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that being a unit attached to the main staff, our task was to enter the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you follow those orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you entered into the town of Srebrenica did you encounter any resistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were there any civilians in Srebrenica when you entered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were civilians, most of them of an advanced age.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Approximately, how many civilians did your unit encounter when you came into the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not very many, not very many civilians. I would not know exactly, but not many.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did you do with those civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally and others who were with me, we told the civilians what we had been told to tell them, that they were to go to the soccer playground in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you also run into a young man who was approximately 30 years old?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me back track one moment. Had you received any orders with regard to what you were supposed to do with civilians that you encountered in the city of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we had been told not to touch them, explicitly told.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milorad Pelemis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were those orders followed in respect to this young man who was about 30 years old?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This Lieutenant Milorad Pelemis ordered again another man to kill that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: To whom did he issue that order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know only his first name and it is Zoran. I do not know his family name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did Zoran obey Lieutenant Pelemis' order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did he do to the young man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He slit his throat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This was a deviation from the orders, the general orders, that you had received previously from Lieutenant Pelemis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was this man who was killed by Zoran the only civilian, male, of military age, that you encountered in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where in the town of Srebrenica did that killing take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was in the centre of the town, but I do not know exactly because that was the first time that I had entered Srebrenica, so I would not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was the body left in plain view in the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Later that same morning, Mr. Erdemovic, did you have an opportunity to see General Mladic in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was ordered by my Commander to go, to return to the entrance into the town where we had come in and to wait, me and two more friends, and when we would see General Mladic arrive, to let Lieutenant Pelemis know about that. I did that when General Mladic passed by.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then did Lieutenant Pelemis either have a conversation with General Mladic or did he do anything in relation to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really do not know that because I did not see them. I was not present when they met and I do not know whether they met at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When did your unit leave Srebrenica and return to Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 12th, around noon, sometime around noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: OK. Mr. Erdemovic, there is for your comfort there is a water pitcher and a glass of water next to you, if you feel you would like to have a glass of water. Are you prepared to proceed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, just a moment, just to calm down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, I now would like to turn your attention to 16th July and ask you whether on that day you and other soldiers in your unit received orders to participate in a special detail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I was not conveyed personally any of those orders, but the Commander who was commanding at the time may have issued that order to somebody about that particular task.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you receive orders at all that day from anybody in relation to a task or a mission that ultimately you went on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: From whom did you receive that orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the group Commander, Brano Gojkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was he of normal rank? I am sorry, let me rephrase that question. Did he normally give your unit orders to perform certain missions or was this an exception?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was an exception. First of all, our detachment was divided into two platoons of Vlasenica and Bijeljina. He was with the Vlasenica one and he issued no orders to the Bijeljina platoon. I do not know about Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, where did your orders normally come from when? I say "your orders", I am talking about the orders that were directed to your unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came from the intelligence centre of the main staff in Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In response to the orders that you received on 16th July, Mr. Erdemovic, where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to Zvornik and Brano Gojkovic and the driver reported to a Lieutenant Colonel whose name I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know what military unit the Lieutenant Colonel was associated with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Lieutenant Colonel, well, the Drina Corps, I should say, because we were in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you see that Lieutenant Colonel wearing any particular uniform with any particular insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, all he had were the insignia of his rank and that is how I knew that he was a Lieutenant Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: OK. Was the Lieutenant Colonel with anyone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he, Brano, and the driver, yes, yes, he was accompanied by two military policemen also from the Corps who had their insignia on the left arm, the insignia of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After there were some conversations between Brano and Lieutenant Colonel, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They told us to sit in the car and to accompany the vehicle with the Lieutenant Colonel and the two military policemen. We went from Zvornik in the direction of Bijeljina, and on the road we stopped at a farm that was at a place called Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, I am going to show you two photographs. I am going to ask you if you recognise what is depicted in each of those photographs. If we could dim the lights and put them on the elmo? Your Honours, we have copies of these as well which we will be submitting to the court. If I could give these to the usher? Let me show you the first exhibit which will be Exhibit No. 63, Mr. Erdemovic. It will be coming up on your screen in just a moment. Do you recognise what is depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a farm -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Lights, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr. Erdemovic. I asked you what is depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the farm where we were taken by this Lieutenant Colonel in the locality called Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, let me show the next photograph which is Exhibit No. 64. Let me ask you, Mr. Erdemovic, do you recognise what is depicted in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do it is the same farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: OK. If we could have the lights on once again, please? After you arrived at that farm, Mr. Erdemovic, did you receive additional orders from your superiors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally did not, but I heard when Brano and the Lieutenant Colonel were talking, saying that buses would be coming to that farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In relation to those buses did you receive any additional information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Afterwards when the Lieutenant Colonel left, Brano said that buses would be coming with Muslims from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he say what you and the members of your unit were supposed to do regarding those Muslims from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That we have to execute those people, to shoot them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say "he" told you you had to shoot them, for the record, who was that, if you could identify him by name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Brano Gojkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You mentioned that members of your unit were present. Can you identify the other members of your unit who were present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can; Franc Kos was present; Goronja Zoran; Savanovic Stanko; Cvetkovic Aleksandar; Boskic Marko; Golijan Vlastimir, myself and Gojkovic Brano.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did buses with civilians from Srebrenica arrive at the farm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Approximately, what time did the first buses arrive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, but I think it was between 9.30 and 10.00 in the morning a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the buses that arrive have any particular markings on them to indicate where they were from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were buses of Sarajevotrans and from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When the first buses arrived, or when the first bus arrived, Mr. Erdemovic, was it filled with men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly whether it was full, but there were men and they were wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you provide to the court the range of ages of these men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, but maybe between 17 and 60 or 70 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On each of those buses carrying these civilians, were there armed escorts, were there people who were carrying guns who were escorting them on the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In each bus, I think, I do not know exactly, but there were two military policemen belonging to the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did these buses arrive one at a time at the farm or did they arrive in large convoys?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: OK. What happened once a bus arrived at the farm? Could you describe what happened, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the bus arrived at the farm, as I said, the Commander of the group, Brano Gojkovic, would tell us how to stand as an execution squad and two military policemen would bring out 10 people of Muslim nationality from Srebrenica at a time, and Brano Gojkovic and Golijan Vlastimir would bring them to the execution squad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Focusing your attention on the first bus, Mr. Erdemovic, were the civilian people who were brought off that bus blindfolded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, only in the first bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How were their hands, were they free or were they tied?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the first bus they were tied only.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I take it in every other bus that came on July 16th the people, the civilians, had neither blindfolds nor were their hands tied; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Once the civilians arrived and were taken off the buses, Mr. Erdemovic, where did they go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They went to the meadow next to the farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where were you and other members of your squad in relation to where the prisoners were brought?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were, I think, about 50 or 100 metres from the buses in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: OK. When the men were brought in your presence, how far away were they from you when they stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think about 20 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were they facing you or were they facing away from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were turned with their backs to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened to those civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were given orders to fire at those civilians, that is, to execute them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you follow that order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but at first I resisted and Brano Gojkovic told me if I was sorry for those people that I should line up with them; and I knew that this was not just a mere threat but that it could happen, because in our unit the situation had become such that the Commander of the group has the right to execute on the spot any individual if he threatens the security of the group or if in any other way he opposes the Commander of the group appointed by the Commander Milorad Pelemis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: OK. Do you know how many buses were brought to Pilica farm on July 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, but I think between 15 and 20 buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the same thing that you have described just a moment ago happen to each one of those bus loads of civilian persons who came off the buses? In other words, were they executed at Pilica farm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: OK. What time, Mr. Erdemovic, did the last bus arrive at the Pilica farm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really do not know exactly what time it was that the last bus arrived, but I know that before the last bus came a group of about 10 soldiers from Bratunac came to the farm, so I cannot know exactly. I do not know what time it was, but maybe around 1530 or 16 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You say a group of soldiers from Bratunac also joined your unit at Pilica farm. Do you know what specific unit they were members of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What unit did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly what unit they belonged to, but I know that they came from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where they members of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did they act in a way that was different to the civilians than the members of your unit acted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they beat the civilians with bars. They said all kinds of things to them. They forced them to kneel and to pray in the Muslim manner, to bow their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did it appear to you, Mr. Erdemovic, that they were attempting to humiliate some of these victims before they killed them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think even that some of them from Bratunac knew some of those victims from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You mentioned, Mr. Erdemovic, that once a bus arrived groups of prisoners, approximately 10, were moved from the buses, taken to a field and executed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who was guarding the remaining civilians who were still on the bus at the time a single group of 10 were being executed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know from which particular unit those military policemen were from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they had the insignia of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, in the course of your time spent at Pilica farm on July 16th, did you have an opportunity to talk one of the victims that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did. It was an elderly man, I think between 50 and 60, and when he was coming out of the bus he started immediately to complain. He said that he had saved Serbs from Srebrenica who were now in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; that he had the telephone numbers of those people and he begged to be allowed to live.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After listening to him what did you do, Mr. Erdemovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said to Brano Gojkovic to let him live, I wanted to save that man. I was sorry for those people simply. I had no reason to shoot at those people. They had done nothing to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What response did you get from Brano Gojkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That he did not want to have any witnesses of that crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he then lead that man away to the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not he, but Golijan Vlastimir did. I quarrelled with them but there was nothing I could do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was the attitude of other members of your particular unit who participated in the executions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the attitude of individual members was almost like mine, that this should not be done, I do not know, whereas individuals did what they did with some kind of revenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were there some members of your unit who boasted about how many people they had killed on July 16th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you expand on that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a man who allegedly or so he said that the Bosnian Muslims had killed his brother who was 17, and he said that he wants his revenge and that on that day he had killed 250 Muslims from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he say that he had counted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Mr. Erdemovic, what was the attitude of the bus drivers who drove the victims to Pilica farm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were horrified. I think those people, those men, did not know that they were being driven to the execution ground. They probably thought they were being led for exchange and that is what this man that I talked to, the one between 50 and 60, actually told me, that it had been promised them. However, Brano Gojkovic entered the bus and gave an automatic rifle, a kalashnikov, and ordered each driver to kill at least one of those Muslims so that they could not testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, Mr. Erdemovic, did any of the military policemen who escorted the men on the buses participate in any of the executions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that day, I do not know -- no, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you estimate, Mr. Erdemovic, how many civilians were killed by your unit and members of the Bratunac unit on 16th July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 16th, somewhere about 1,000, 1,200, I do not know. I estimated the number according to the arrivals of the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: OK. Are you able to estimate how many people you killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly. I cannot estimate but, to be quite frank, I would rather not know how many people I killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: OK. Mr. Erdemovic, did you receive any information on 16th July about what was going to happen to the bodies of the victims that were lying in the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the Lieutenant Colonel arrived at the end, one of the guards who was there on the farm who was watching the farm said that those victims would probably be buried there, and that trench diggers would come to dig them into the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he say when those trench diggers would come to the farm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You mentioned, Mr. Erdemovic, that the Lieutenant Colonel who you had seen earlier that morning returned to the farm after or during the course of the executions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he came at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In your opinion, did he see the dead bodies that were covering the field?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, yes, he saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he make any comments about seeing those bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. He made no comments, but he said in the place of Pilica there were another 500 of those Muslims from Srebrenica and that we had to go to finish off that work. I said aloud that I would not, that I did not wish to kill anyone, that I was no robot for the extermination of people. Then I was supported by some individuals from my unit so we did not go, but the group from Bratunac went.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Mr. Erdemovic, could you name the other members of your unit who supported your refusal to participate in additional killings in the town of Pilica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Kos Franc, Boskic Marko and Goronja Zoran.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, why did you refuse to follow that additional order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I just could not take it any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: OK. You mentioned, Mr. Erdemovic, that other soldiers accepted to follow that order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The soldiers from Bratunac went immediately with the Lieutenant Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know where they went?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard when the Lieutenant Colonel said that in the hall in Pilica there were 500 Muslims who were trying to break through the door and get out of the hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you eventually on that same day, Mr. Erdemovic, travel to Pilica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Brano Gojkovic said that the Lieutenant Colonel had told him that he had to hold a meeting in Pilica later. We went where the Lieutenant Colonel said we should go, and it was not far from the hall or actually across the street from it. When we got there, where we were told to report, I heard shots and, how can I put it, hand grenades which went off in the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How far were you from that particular building, Mr. Erdemovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some 70 to 100 metres, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Erdemovic, if people were killed inside that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably they were killed, as soon as the shots could be heard and the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: OK. Mr. Erdemovic, after the events that you have just described in Pilica, did your unit eventually return to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, we went to Vlasenica, and they told us then that they were free and that our platoon, which was from Bijeljina, could go back to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you return to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then eventually did you return home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, shortly after the killings of Pilica farm, and after you had returned home, were you shot by a member of the 10th Sabotage unit who had participated in the massacres at Pilica farm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you suffer extremely serious injuries as a result of that shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Which of the members of the 10th Sabotage unit shot you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The man who bragged that he had killed most Muslims, Savanovic Stanko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, I have concluded my examination of Mr. Erdemovic. Thank you, Mr. Erdemovic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you have any questions? Mr. Erdemovic, the Prosecutor has done with his questions. The Judges might have a few questions. Would you rather that we have a recess before we address those questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I would rather your Honours gets this over with as soon as possible because I am finding it very hard.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is what I thought, in fact. So, Judge Riad, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, when you entered Srebrenica, you said that you found a few number of people and mainly old people. Were there any armed people in Srebrenica when you entered and what was their percentage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was not a single armed man, nor was there any resistance when we entered the city.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: You mentioned the case of the man which has been butchered in front of your eyes. What was the reason for the choice of this man? Was it to give an example to the population, or did he commit something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really do not know why, why precisely this was done, but I think it was done because that man was able for military service.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Did you during all this period see General Mladic or hear him cited by others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only saw him drive past in the car, as I said, when he entered the city of Srebrenica. I did not personally hear him issuing any orders and I heard from people that they had seen him.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I am sorry to go back to the executions. Did you make sure, your troop, that everybody was executed before you left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally, I did not and I do not think that most of those men would check because this was really something awful. I do not know. We did not check.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: This is my last question. You said that after you left Pilica farm you were shot at by this man called Stanko. Why did he shoot at you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my assumption is that someone, one of those men (and I think it was Gojkovic Brano), had conveyed to the Commander of my unit my behaviour at the farm and that probably they had reached the conclusion that I just could not stand it and that, perhaps, I do not know, that I might do what I am doing today, that is, testifying against it.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Could you briefly tell us what happened to you after you were shot at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was not just me that was shot at but two other colleagues who were also opposed to the orders of the Commander and some other people in our unit. What saved me, who saved me was a man who was Deputy Commander of our unit. He asked the doctors when they took me to the hospital to operate me immediately, but the operation in Bijeljina did not succeed. Then he again begged the doctors and explained the circumstances under which I was wounded, and how it had happened and that he too had been wounded and another colleague of ours and that I be transferred to the Military Hospital in Belgrade and the doctors did so.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Sorry to add this, you mentioned that in April 1994 you joined the army of Bosnian Serbs. You, being a Croat, what pushed you to join this army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was quite awful. First, I was in the army of the Bosnian Muslims, then of the Bosnian Croats and at the end of the Bosnian Serbs. I did not want to join the army, but I had no other choice. I had to join the army to have somewhere to stay, because I had my wife with me who was pregnant and that was the only motive, I did not have anywhere to go, to join the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Erdemovic, two questions: what weapon did you have on you at the time of the execution? Did you have a gun, a rifle, a machine gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An ordinary automatic rifle, a kalashnikov.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: So people were shot down by vollies of fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, at least, no, I fired individual shots.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: My last question. Why did you want to testify? What feeling underlies that and what do you feel now that you are before the International Criminal Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wanted to testify because of my conscience, because of all that happened because I did not want that. I was simply compelled to, forced to, and I could choose between my life and the life of those people; and had I lost my life then, that would not have changed the fate of those people. The fate of those people was decided by somebody holding a much higher position than I did. As I have said already, what really got me, I mean, it has completely destroyed my life and that is why I testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions of Mr. Erdemovic and I would like to thank Mr. Erdemovic for testifying here today.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The court is going to adjourn until quarter past 5. (4.50 p.m.) (The court adjourned for a short time). (5.15 p.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Counsel for the Prosecution, it is Friday, 5th July, 1715 hours. What does the rest of the day look like, given the changes that have been made due to circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have one additional witness to call and we have a statement that we would like to read into the record and we have a number of exhibits which we will tender. First of all, your Honour I would like to tender the two photographs that were identified by the previous witness Exhibits 63 and 64. Then I have a series of transcripts that I would like to tender but have not yet been given numbers and I will tender those at the conclusion, if that please the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What transcripts are we talking about sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am talking about a transcript of James Gow that was of his testimony in the Nikolic Rule 61 hearing; the transcript of James Gow's testimony in the Vukovar Rule 61 hearing and then certain testimonies of certain witnesses from the Tadic trial.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK, fine, these are transcripts relating to other hearings and which you would like to tender. I do not think there any problem with that. So we will accept the two photographs as Exhibits. Now with regard to the rest of our deliberations, we will be hearing the last witness. Thereafter -- Mr. Harmon does not need a head set apparently -- so we are going to hear the last witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We are going to hear your statement. I think that we will be able to adjourn this evening and hear your final remarks Monday morning at 10 o'clock. Would that suit you?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So we would not be sitting tomorrow morning. Gentlemen, can you agree with that fine?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I know that my fellow Judges can go along with that as well. So, you have the floor, Mr. Ostberg, till 6 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour I would like to call our last witness and that is the Chief of Police of the City of Tuzla. Mr. Pasaga Mesic, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can you hear me sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In translation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So please read the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You have been called as a witness by the Prosecution. So I am going to ask Mr. Ostberg to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Will you please state your name and also spell it for the record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pasaga Mesic, P-A-S-A-G-A M-E-S-I-C.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Would you also state your present occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Head of the Police Department in Tuzla which, among other things, collects facts about crimes committed in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Could you tell us about what this Police Department in Tuzla encompassed, the cities or places we have been talking about in the context of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My Department covered the territory of northeast Bosnia. Before the war there was the administrative Tuzla, it belonged to Tuzla region which, among other common municipalities, covers the municipalities of Srebrenica, Bratunac and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you in your office try to identify missing people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: How did you go about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did it in several ways. The chief method was that when people expelled from Srebrenica arrived, when the Serb Army took the enclave of Srebrenica in those places where the expelled were accommodated in their settlements, we conducted a questionnaire of all citizens of age who had arrived there. The questionnaire included, in addition to the name and particulars, it also included a question of where their next of kin were. In those questionnaires they listed the names of their close relatives who either had been kept by the Serb Army in Potocari or tried to reach the free territory through the woods. Another question in the questionnaire was whether they had witnessed a murder or some other crime, that is some other violation of International Humanitarian Law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you provide the Court with a figure of numbers of missing people from the UN safe area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After we collected all the information and facts in this and other ways, we can make some estimates about the number of persons missing. It is, however, still impossible to identify all the missing persons. The information we have gathered so far says that during the attack of the Serb Army against the enclave, the protected zone of Srebrenica, between 6,000 to 6500 people disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What means did you use to reach this result, apart from what you already told us about this questionnaire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In addition to this we also used lists of missing persons compiled by the ICRC, and that is their office in Tuzla which was also supplied to the Commission for the exchange of prisoners in Tuzla. We also used information from the lists of missing persons compiled by representatives of the municipalities Srebrenica, Bratunac and Vlasenica. On the basis of all this information and by subtracting from that number persons who arrived in the free territory in the meantime, including the surrender of persons to IFOR in Zvornik, it was 3,469 (sic) missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Will you name the figure again I did not quite get it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now during this period the three territory was reached by a certain number of members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina who managed to break through the Serb blockade. We do not have the exact figure because it is a military secret and, therefore, may not be divulged but on the basis of the information we have, we estimate that it is about 30 per cent of the last figure I mentioned, which also means that about 3,000 to 3,500 members of the Army arrived in the free territory, and when this is subtracted from those 9,349 we arrive at the first figure, that is that about 6,000 to 6,500 people are still missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would like to turn to another matter, namely photographs which I am soon going to show you. I will first ask you this. Did the Office of the Prosecutor present you with photographs of prisoners from the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Do you know where these photographs came from? Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.Pages 860 to 877.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know that, but I know that the photographs were taken of a film which was in the possession of an investigating team of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. What were you asked to do with these photos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The investigators team of the Tribunal asked us to try to identify those persons with those who had arrived in the territory, as they were showing men who were members of the Serb Army in Potocari and other places in the Srebrenica area were separated by the Serb Army from the their families and taken in an unknown direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What methods did you use to try to identify these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We began by showing those photographs to expelled from Srebrenica in refugee camps in which they were away accommodated, but since they were scattered all over the territory, almost across the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina of those expelled, we were not able to identify them for those missing persons. A fortnight ago we used a cantonal television of Tuzla and we broadcasted those photographs and invited all those who could recognise any one person from those photographs to some to our office and then identify any one of those persons they could recognise or they knew from the photographs that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. How many photographs were you presented with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were shown 30 photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Were you able to determine the identities of the persons of these photos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we identified 28 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I am going to show you some photos and you can tell us what you found out concerning the people we are going to show you. I think there are in total 16 photos and the first one is Exhibit 8(A). Can the Court see the photograph also? I now ask you, can you identify any persons on that photo, or were you able to identify any one of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this photograph we identified three persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Can we ask you to dim the lights. Thank you. Please proceed. Again my question was, can you identify any one of these people on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the person I am pointing at now is Sevko Mujic, the son of Omer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Do you have a pointer? Has he something to point with? On the elmo I think you have to do it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The person I am pointing at now is Sevko Mujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Who identified him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was identified by a neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Can you tell us about his fate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He disappeared. He is missing and nothing is known about his fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any other persons on this photo that you can identify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Who is this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is Ahmo Mehmedovic, the son of Sulejman, aged 58. He was identified by a neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: His fate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is also missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Any others on this photo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This person here, this is Meho Mehmedovic, the son of Sulejman, Ahmo's brother, aged 56, identified by neighbours too.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: His fate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is missing too.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. As your Honours may recall, these are photos that were shown by our investigator, Rene Ruez, during his examination. As you have seen them before and now we have shown them again just for this purpose. Can I have Exhibit No. 8(B), please? Can you identify anybody on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is this person. He was also on Exhibit 8(A) and this is Meho Mehmedovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: And who identified him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was identified by a neighbour or rather two persons who were his neighbours while they were in the area of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What do we know about him today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: May I now have Exhibit No. 10(B). Can you identify anybody on this photo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, please, and that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This person's name is Kasim Hafizovic, the son of Mehmed, aged 58, identified by his close relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: What do we know about him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is missing too.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Is there anybody else on this photo you can identify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Senahid Hafizovic, Mehmed's son, aged 54, also identified by neighbours and he is also on the list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go on to Exhibit No. 11(A). We can readily see two persons on it. Can you identify them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This person here is Mesa Efendic, son of Meho, aged 63, identified by a neighbour, also on the list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: The other one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The other person is Ibro Huseinovic, the son of Ahmo, aged 51, identified by his close relatives on the list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Can we now, please, go to Exhibit No. 12(D)? I cannot see anything on my screen for the moment. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This person was identified on this photograph. This is Nazif Krdzic, aged 54, identified by a colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: His fate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is missing too.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Now please we go to Exhibit No. 13(A). Could you point to some of the people there? Yes, and who is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is Bajro Malkic, son of Hilmo, aged 53, identified by his relatives on the list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other people on this photo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next person is Mevludin Pasagic, aged 56, identified by his close relatives on the list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The other person on this photograph is Hamza Gurdic, aged 52, identified by colleagues and he is also on the list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I will ask for No. 13(B).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here we again see Hamza Gurdic that we saw in Exhibit 13(A). Then this person here whose name is Idriz Suljic the son of Saban, aged 60, identified by friends on the list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This person here is Ibrahim Jelkic, the son of Bahrija, aged 59, identified by a friend also on the list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I now ask for Exhibit No. 14(B). You will recognise him. That was the person who was forced to call out for his comrades in the hills. Yes, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This person here is Ramo Osmanovic, the son of Omer, aged 42, identified by relatives on the list of missing persons. This photograph too we have identified this person here, and this is Miralem Mujic, the son of Rasim, aged 47, identified by close relatives, also on the list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I have Exhibit No. 15(B)? You do also, your Honours, recognise him. He was the person who was interviewed by a television reporter. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This person is Ramo Mustafic, son of Meho, aged 54, identified by relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I will ask for Exhibit No. 16(A).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this photograph we see Salih Salihovic, aged 49, identified by friends on the list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask for No. 17(B)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here we identified two persons: This is Ramo Kabilovic, the son of Hajro, aged 34, identified by close relatives on the list of missing persons. In the middle and behind him on the stretcher is Mujo Mesanovic, son of Abdulah, aged 22, identified by close relatives on the list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask for Exhibit No. 18(A)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This person is Salih Ibisevic, son of Ibrahim, 36 years old, identified by his close relatives on the list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Now 19(B), please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this photograph this young man has been identified. His name is Almir Salcinovic, son of Turabija, 21 years old, identified by a friend. Then Halil Gabeljic, son of Mahmut, identified by a friend, also on the list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Both of these people are missing, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: That takes us to 20(B), please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This person's name is Muhamed Malagic, son of Ramiz, 23 years old, identified by his close relatives on the list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Now 21(B), please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this photograph Nezir Ibisevic has been identified. He is son of Juso, 20 years old. He was identified by his friends. He is on the missing persons list.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we are going to show you the last photograph, and that is 22(B).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This person's name is by Bajazit Delic, son of Amil. He was identified by distant relatives and is on the missing persons list. This is Mustafa Mujcinovic, son of Mujo, 38 years old identified by an acquaintance on the missing persons list.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. To sum it up, all these people we now have photos, are they all missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all these persons are on the missing persons list. We said that 28 persons were identified, we saw 26 persons because two persons reached free territory and their photographs for security reasons we will not be showing. One man is 62 years old and a boy who is only 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you. All the others are missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, very much. This concludes the questions I have to put to you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You have a question madam Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: Thank you just one

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Mr. Pasaga Mesic, you spoke of about 6,000, 6,500 missing persons. Could you tell the Court how many are men, how many are women, how many are children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
